title: WHY DID GOD COMMAND ISRAEL TO DESTROY CERTAIN GIANT TRIBES?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD COMMAND ISRAEL TO DESTROY CERTAIN GIANT TRIBES?
The Question That Makes Many Christians Uncomfortable
There are passages in Scripture that inspire us.
There are passages that comfort us.
And then there are passages that stop us cold.
Pages that make us shift in our seat.
Pages we secretly hope nobody asks us about.
This is one of them.
When readers encounter God's commands concerning the destruction of certain giant tribes—the Anakim, Rephaim, Emim, Zamzummim, and others—the immediate reaction is often emotional.
Why would a loving God command this?
Why were entire giant peoples removed from the land?
Was this genocide?
Was God acting differently in the Old Testament than in the New?
And perhaps most honestly:
How do I reconcile these passages with the Jesus who said, "Love your enemies"?
These are not shallow questions.
They deserve serious answers.
Not emotional reactions.
Not internet myths.
Not sensational theories.
But careful Scripture.
Because the deeper we look, the more astonishing the story becomes.
The Giants Were Never the Main Story
Most people imagine the giants as merely unusually tall humans.
The Bible presents something far stranger.
The story begins long before Israel ever entered Canaan.
In Genesis 6:4 we read:
"The Nephilim were on the earth in those days—and also afterward—when the sons of God came in to the daughters of men and they bore children to them."
The Hebrew text reads:

הַנְּפִלִים
(ha-nephilim)
"Nephilim"
The word likely derives from the Hebrew root נפל (naphal), meaning "to fall."
Thus many scholars understand Nephilim as "fallen ones" or beings associated with a supernatural rebellion.
The text immediately connects them with:

בְּנֵי הָאֱלֹהִים
(b'nei ha'elohim)
"Sons of God"
Throughout the Old Testament, this phrase consistently refers to heavenly beings rather than ordinary humans (Job 1:6; Job 2:1; Job 38:7).

The earliest Jewish interpreters, including the writers of the Dead Sea Scrolls and many Second Temple Jewish sources, understood Genesis 6 as describing a supernatural rebellion involving divine beings and human women.
The result was an unnatural offspring.
The Bible does not dwell on every detail.
But it does identify these beings as:

הַגִּבֹּרִים
(hagibborim)
"The mighty ones."
This rebellion becomes one of the reasons God sends the Flood.
The Flood Was Not Merely Judgment on Human Sin
Most people understand Noah's Flood as God's response to widespread wickedness.
That is true.
But Genesis presents another layer.
Creation itself had become corrupted.
Violence covered the earth.
Humanity was being destroyed spiritually and morally.
The boundaries God established in creation were being violated.
The Flood was not merely punishment.
It was a cleansing.
A reset.
A preservation of God's redemptive plan through Noah.
Yet Genesis contains a haunting phrase:
"And also afterward."
The giant clans reappear.
Not as a worldwide civilization.
But concentrated in specific regions.
Particularly in Canaan.
The Land Filled With Giant Tribes
When Israel approached the Promised Land, the spies reported:
"We saw the Nephilim there."
(Numbers 13:33)
The descendants of Anak.
The Anakim.
The Rephaim.
The Emim.
The Zamzummim.
These were not scattered individuals.
They were established peoples occupying strategic territories.
Deuteronomy repeatedly references them as unusually powerful giant clans.
The Hebrew term often associated with them is:

רְפָאִים
(Rephaim)
A mysterious people remembered throughout the Old Testament.
Ancient Israel viewed these groups as more than military threats.
They represented the continuation of an ancient rebellion against God's created order.
The Battle Was Not About Height
This is where modern readers often miss the point.
The issue was never simply that these people were tall.
If height were the problem, Scripture would condemn every tall person.
It does not.
God later uses giant individuals for His purposes.
The issue was what these tribes represented.
The Bible consistently presents Canaan as a center of extraordinary corruption.
Child sacrifice.
Temple prostitution.
Ritual violence.
Occult practices.
Demonic worship.
God had waited centuries before judgment came.
Genesis 15:16 records God telling Abraham:
"For the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete."
Think about that.
God waited over four hundred years.
Four centuries of patience.
Four centuries of mercy.
Four centuries before judgment finally arrived.
The God of Scripture is never impulsive.
Judgment comes only after generations of rebellion.
The Meaning of "Herem"
One of the most misunderstood concepts in these passages is the Hebrew word:

חֵרֶם
(herem)
Often translated as "devote to destruction."
Modern readers hear annihilation.
Ancient Israelites heard something different.
Something sacred.
Something judicial.
Herem referred to placing something entirely under God's judgment.
It was not ordinary warfare.
It was not conquest for wealth.
It was not ethnic cleansing.
Israel was specifically forbidden from enriching itself through many of these campaigns.
The land was not being cleansed because of race.
It was being judged because of rebellion.
This distinction matters enormously.
The Judgment Was Never Ethnic
One fact completely destroys the idea that God was judging people because of ethnicity.
Many Canaanites were spared.
Some became heroes of faith.
Rahab.
A Canaanite prostitute.
She believed.
She was saved.
She entered the Messianic line.
Ruth.
A Moabite.
She became the great-grandmother of David.
Entire groups such as the Gibeonites survived because they sought peace.
The determining factor was never bloodline.
It was allegiance.
Repentance always opened the door to mercy.
Always.
Even in the Old Testament.
Especially in the Old Testament.
The Cosmic War Behind the Story
The biblical narrative reveals something larger than human politics.
From Eden onward, Scripture describes a conflict between God's kingdom and rebellious spiritual powers.
After Babel, Deuteronomy 32 describes the nations being allotted under heavenly rulers.
Many became corrupt.
Psalm 82 portrays God judging these rebellious spiritual authorities.
The giant clans emerge within this broader context.
They become earthly manifestations of a deeper spiritual rebellion.
This is why the conquest narratives feel different from ordinary wars.
They are not merely geopolitical conflicts.
They are episodes in a cosmic struggle over the future of God's redemptive plan.
Protecting the Line of the Messiah
One reality often overlooked is that Scripture is telling one continuous story.
From Genesis to Revelation.
A story leading toward Jesus Christ.
Immediately after humanity falls, God promises:
"And I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your seed and her seed."
(Genesis 3:15)
This becomes the first Messianic prophecy.
The promised Deliverer would come.
The serpent would try to stop Him.
Throughout Scripture, attempts arise to corrupt, destroy, or eliminate the covenant line.
The giant clans appear within that larger storyline.
The preservation of Israel was not merely about national survival.
It was about preserving the path through which the Messiah would come.
If Israel vanished, so would the promises.
If the covenant line disappeared, so would humanity's hope.
The Cross Changes Everything
Many ask why these judgments seem absent in the New Testament.
The answer is found at Calvary.
The judgment that fell on rebellious humanity ultimately fell upon Christ.
The Greek New Testament uses the word:

χάρις
(charis)
Grace.
Undeserved favor.
The cross becomes the place where justice and mercy meet.
God did not abandon judgment.
He absorbed it Himself.
The same God who judged Canaan stretched out His hands on a Roman cross.
The same God who confronted evil bore evil's penalty.
The same God who demanded holiness became the sacrifice for sinners.
This is not two different Gods.
It is one story.
One plan.
One redemption.
The Question We Rarely Ask
When reading these passages, we often ask:
"Why did God judge them?"
Scripture quietly asks a different question.
"Why does God continue to show mercy to us?"
The real miracle is not that judgment came.
The miracle is how long it waited.
The miracle is that God warned.
The miracle is that God provided escape.
The miracle is that Rahab found mercy.
The miracle is that sinners like us can find mercy too.
The Giants Are Gone. The Battle Remains.
Most believers will never face an Anakim warrior.
Most will never see a Rephaim king.
But every believer still faces the deeper conflict.
The battle between truth and deception.
Faith and fear.
Holiness and compromise.
Christ and the kingdoms of darkness.
The giant tribes are gone.
The spiritual war remains.
And yet the ending has already been written.
When Jesus rose from the grave, He accomplished what Israel's warriors never could.
A final victory.
A permanent victory.
An eternal victory.
The last giant has already fallen.
His name was death.
And Christ crushed him beneath an empty tomb.
If this article challenged something you've always assumed about Scripture, save it and revisit the passages yourself.
The God who judged evil is the same God who chose to bear its punishment Himself.
